'''Robert Eric Betzig''' (born January 13, 1960) is an [[Americans|American]] [[physicist]] who works as a professor of physics and professor of molecular and cell biology at the [[University of California, Berkeley]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://physics.berkeley.edu/people/faculty/eric-betzig|title=Eric Betzig {{!}} UC Berkeley Physics|website=physics.berkeley.edu|access-date=July 18, 2019|archive-date=January 18, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210118102010/https://physics.berkeley.edu/people/faculty/eric-betzig|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://vcresearch.berkeley.edu/faculty/eric-betzig|title=Eric Betzig {{!}} Research UC Berkeley|website=vcresearch.berkeley.edu|access-date=July 18, 2019|archive-date=April 13, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210413215502/https://vcresearch.berkeley.edu/faculty/eric-betzig|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=https://www.hhmi.org/scientists/eric-betzig|title=Eric Betzig|website=HHMI.org|language=en|access-date=July 18, 2019|archive-date=May 6, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210506175609/https://www.hhmi.org/scientists/eric-betzig|url-status=live}}</ref> He is also a senior fellow at the [[Janelia Farm Research Campus]] in [[Ashburn, Virginia]].<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /><ref name="hhmi">{{cite web|url=http://www.hhmi.org/scientists/eric-betzig|title=Eric Betzig, PhD|work=hhmi.org|publisher=[[Howard Hughes Medical Institute]]|access-date=October 8, 2014|archive-date=October 10, 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141010120254/http://www.hhmi.org/scientists/eric-betzig|url-status=live}}</ref>

Betzig has worked to develop the field of [[fluorescence microscopy]] and [[photoactivated localization microscopy]]. He was awarded the 2014 [[Nobel Prize in Chemistry]] for "the development of super-resolved fluorescence microscopy"<ref name="nobel">{{cite news |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/chemistry/laureates/2014/press.html |title=The Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2014 |work=Nobelprize.org |publisher=Nobel Media AB |date=October 8, 2014 |access-date=October 8, 2014 |archive-date=May 2, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180502031322/https://www.nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/chemistry/laureates/2014/press.html |url-status=live }}</ref> along with [[Stefan Hell]] and fellow Cornell alumnus [[W. E. Moerner|William E. Moerner]].<ref name="hhmipr">{{cite web |url=http://www.hhmi.org/news/eric-betzig-wins-2014-nobel-prize-chemistry |title=Eric Betzig Wins 2014 Nobel Prize in Chemistry |work=HHMI News |publisher=hhmi.org |date=October 8, 2014 |access-date=October 8, 2014 |archive-date=October 10, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141010120511/http://www.hhmi.org/news/eric-betzig-wins-2014-nobel-prize-chemistry |url-status=live }}</ref>

[[File:GFP Superresolution Christoph Cremer.JPG|thumb|300px| Dual color localization microscopy SPDMphymod/super-resolution microscopy with GFP & RFP fusion proteins]]

==Early life and education==

Betzig was born in [[Ann Arbor, Michigan]], in 1960, the son of Helen Betzig and engineer Robert Betzig. Aspiring to work in the aerospace industry, Betzig studied [[physics]] at the [[California Institute of Technology]] and graduated with a [[Bachelor of Science|BS]] degree in 1983. He then went on to study at [[Cornell University]] where Michael Isaacson was his supervisor, and he also worked with Aaron Lewis. There he obtained an [[Master of Science|MS]] degree and a [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]] degree in [[applied physics]] and [[engineering physics]] in 1985 and 1988, respectively. For his PhD he focused on developing high-resolution optical microscopes that could see past the theoretical limit of 0.2 micrometers.<ref name="janelia" /><ref name=twisting>{{cite news|last1=Feltman|first1=Rachel|title=Nobel chemistry laureate's twisting path to molecular microscope breakthrough|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/national/health-science/nobel-chemistry-laureates-twisting-path-to-molecular-microscope-breakthrough/2014/10/08/f06d6a2e-4e75-11e4-8c24-487e92bc997b_story.html|access-date=August 19, 2015|newspaper=Washington Post|date=October 8, 2014}}</ref><ref name="thesis-betzig-1988">{{cite thesis |title=Nondestructive optical imaging of surfaces with 500 angstrom resolution |date=1988 |publisher=[[Cornell University]] |type=Ph.D. |last=Betzig |first=Robert Eric |url=https://www.proquest.com/docview/303699541|id={{ProQuest|303699541}} |url-access=subscription  |oclc=79223216}}</ref>

==Career==

===Bell Laboratories===
After receiving his doctorate, Betzig was hired by [[Bell Labs|AT&T Bell Laboratories]] in the Semiconductor Physics Research Department in 1989. That year Betzig's colleague, William E. Moerner, developed the first optical microscope that could see past the .2 micrometer limit, known as the [[Abbe limit]], but it could only function at temperatures near [[absolute zero]].  Inspired by Moerner's research, Betzig became the first person to image individual fluorescent molecules at room temperature while determining their positions within less than .2 micrometers in 1993. For this he received the [[William O. Baker Award for Initiatives in Research]] (previously known as the National Academy of Sciences Award for Initiatives in Research).<ref name="janelia">{{cite web |url=https://www.janelia.org/people/scientist/eric-betzig |title=Eric Betzig |work=janelia.org |publisher=[[Janelia Farm Research Campus]] |access-date=October 8, 2014 |archive-date=April 30, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150430215620/http://janelia.org/people/scientist/eric-betzig |url-status=live }}</ref>  Betzig was also awarded the [[William L. McMillan]] Award in 1992.<ref>{{cite web | title=McMillan Award | website=Department of Physics at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign | date= | url=https://physics.illinois.edu/people/honors-and-awards/mcmillan-award | access-date=December 8, 2023}}</ref>

===Ann Arbor Machine Company===
In 1994, Betzig became frustrated with the academic community and the uncertainty of the corporate structure of Bell Laboratories, prompting him to leave both. He spent some years as a [[stay-at-home dad]] before reentering the workforce in 1996, when he took up the position of vice president of [[research and development]] at Ann Arbor Machine Company, which was partially owned by the Betzig family.<ref name=ars>{{cite news|last1=Timmer|first1=John|title=Quitting + failures + a microscope in the living room = Nobel Prize|url=https://arstechnica.com/science/2015/04/quitting-failures-a-microscope-in-the-living-room-nobel-prize/|access-date=August 19, 2015|work=ars technicia|date=April 10, 2015}}</ref><ref name="hhmipr" /> Here he developed Flexible Adaptive Servohydraulic Technology (FAST), but after spending millions of dollars on development he only sold two devices.<ref name="janelia" /><ref name=twisting /><ref name=ars /><ref name="nature">{{Cite journal | last1 = Gewin | first1 = Virginia | s2cid = 143733760 | year = 2006 | title = Eric Betzig, group leader, Janelia Farm Research Campus, Howard Hughes Medical Institute, Leesburg, Virginia | journal = Nature | volume = 440 | issue =  7083| pages = 578 | doi = 10.1038/nj7083-578a | doi-access = free }}</ref>

===Return to academia===
In 2002, Betzig returned to the field of microscopy and founded New Millennium Research in [[Okemos, Michigan]]. Inspired by [[Michael W. Davidson|Mike Davidson]]'s work with fluorescent proteins, he developed photoactivated localization microscopy (PALM), a method of controlling fluorescent proteins that used pulses of light to create images of a higher resolution than were previously thought possible. In the living room of his old Bell Labs collaborator [[Harald Hess]], Betzig and Hess developed the first optical microscope based on this technology. They built their first prototype in under two months, earning them widespread attention. In October of that year, the [[Howard Hughes Medical Institute]]'s [[Janelia Farm Research Campus]] hired him, but his lab was still under construction at the time.<ref name=twisting />

In early 2006, he formally joined Janelia as a group leader to work on developing [[Super-resolution microscopy|super high-resolution fluorescence microscopy]] techniques. He used this technique to study the division of cells in human embryos.<ref name="hhmipr" /><ref name=washingtonpost1>{{cite news|last1=Feltman|first1=Rachel|title=The Nobel Prize in chemistry goes to three men who revolutionized microscopy|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/speaking-of-science/wp/2014/10/08/the-nobel-prize-in-chemistry-goes-to-three-men-who-revolutionized-microscopy/|access-date=August 19, 2015|newspaper=Washington Post|date=October 8, 2014}}</ref> In 2010, he was offered the [[Max Delbruck Prize]], but he declined it and [[Xiaowei Zhuang]] received the award. In 2014, Betzig was jointly awarded the [[Nobel Prize in Chemistry]] along with [[Stefan Hell]] and [[W. E. Moerner|William E. Moerner]].<ref name="nobel" /><ref name=twisting /><ref>{{cite web|title=EricBetzig: Chemist and Nobel Prize|url=https://www.starmus.com/dt_team/eric-betzig/|publisher=Starmus|access-date=August 19, 2015}}</ref>
[[File:Eric Betzig 2018.jpg|thumb|Eric Betzig at the Pontifical Academy of Sciences, November 14, 2018]]
On May 31, 2016, he was appointed an Academician of the [[Pontifical Academy of Sciences]] by [[Pope Francis]].

In the summer of 2017, Betzig joined the [[UC Berkeley|Berkeley]] faculty with a joint appointment at [[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory]].<ref name="berkeleynews">{{cite news|last1=Israel|first1=Brett|title=Nobel Prize winner to join UC Berkeley faculty|url=http://news.berkeley.edu/2016/09/27/nobel-prize-winner-to-join-uc-berkeley-faculty/|access-date=September 28, 2016|publisher=Berkeley News|date=September 27, 2016}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Betzig has married twice. His first wife was [[condensed matter physics|condensed matter physicist]] {{ill|Ruby Ghosh|qid=Q124259081|short=1}},<ref name="thesis-betzig-1988" /> with whom he has two sons, Cayden and Ravi.<ref name=angewandte2015>{{cite journal | last=Betzig | first=Eric | title=Single Molecules, Cells, and Super-Resolution Optics (Nobel Lecture) | journal=Angewandte Chemie International Edition | volume=54 | issue=28 | date=July 6, 2015 | issn=1433-7851 | doi=10.1002/anie.201501003 | pages=8034–8053 | pmid=26087684 | bibcode=2015ACIE...54.8034B |quote="I'm also lucky in that I have a second chance to be a better husband and father. While IÏm close with Kriya and Ravi, one of my regrets is that I didnÏt spend more time with them when they were growing up. Na and I have two happy and beautiful little hellions, Max and Mia, and I have the opportunity to be with them more. I donÏt know, though, if IÏll ever figure out how to optimally balance my responsibility and desire to be at both work and home."}}</ref> His second wife is [[biophysics|biophysicist]] [[Na Ji]],<ref name="berkeleynews" /> with whom he has three children, Max, Mia and Zoe.<ref name= angewandte2015/>
